intro.why: Language models know a lot but store it opaquely and can hallucinate. Knowledge graphs store facts explicitly, with meanings machines can reason over, and are increasingly combined with LLMs (M14) to ground answers in checkable facts.

sections.title: Syntactic vs semantic search
sections.plain: Matching strings is not the same as matching meaning.
sections.body:
Tell a friend "I bought an apple; it cost me 80,000" and they instantly know it's a phone, not fruit, because they know typical prices. A keyword engine doesn't: it matches the string "apple".

Syntactic search ranks by shared words, so "cheap laptop repair" may miss "Affordable computer hardware fixes" (no shared words) and prefer "Laptop bags: cheap deals". Semantic search uses meaning: synonyms (cheap ≈ affordable), types (a laptop is a computer), relations and context. Modern engines combine embeddings (M2–M3, M14) with structured knowledge.

Even "The Glass Palace, Amitav Ghosh, HarperCollins, 2000, London" lets a person infer it's a book: an author and a publisher imply one. The Semantic Web vision is to publish data with explicit, shared, machine-readable meaning so programs can make such inferences, and connected facts can ground AI systems and reduce hallucination.

sections.title: RDF triples and graph traversal
sections.plain: Write every fact as subject–predicate–object; facts sharing a node join into a graph.
sections.body:
The Resource Description Framework represents knowledge as triples (subject, predicate, object), with things named by URIs (global identifiers) so data from different sources can link up.

"Rahul ordered a Margherita; the Margherita costs 250; the Margherita is veg" becomes (Rahul, ordered, Margherita), (Margherita, hasPrice, 250), (Margherita, isOfType, Veg). Triples sharing "Margherita" form a graph. Questions become walks: what did Rahul order? (1 hop); how much did it cost? (2 hops: Rahul → Margherita → 250); who ordered something veg? (reverse traversal).

Limitation: RDF fixes the format, not the meaning. One dataset says "ordered", another "bought", a third "placedOrderFor"; a query for "ordered" finds one order in three until all are mapped to a shared vocabulary (e.g. schema.org terms).

sections.title: RDFS: classes and types
sections.plain: Add a blueprint layer: which kinds of things exist, which belong to which kind, and how kinds nest.
sections.body:
RDF Schema adds vocabulary for describing data: rdfs:Class (a kind of thing), rdf:type (an instance belongs to a class: Ram rdf:type Customer), rdfs:subClassOf (Pizza ⊑ Food ⊑ Product), plus domain and range for properties.

Like an architect's blueprint for a building, the schema says what can exist and how parts relate. It also enables inference: from Margherita rdf:type Pizza and Pizza ⊑ Food ⊑ Product, a system derives Margherita rdf:type Food and rdf:type Product without anyone stating them.

Templates: a student graph uses the same pattern for every student (Student studies Subject; Subject belongsTo Department; Student studiesAt College; College locatedIn City; City locatedIn State …). Shared nodes (the same college, the same city) connect many students, which is what makes graph queries powerful.

sections.title: Ontologies: classes, instances and properties
sections.plain: A formal, shared description of a domain's concepts and how they relate.
sections.body:
An ontology specifies a domain's classes (concepts), instances (individuals), and properties (relations between things, or attributes), along with hierarchies and constraints.

Sandwich ontology: class Sandwich, with subclasses VegSandwich and NonVegSandwich; Sandwich madeOf Ingredient; Sandwich usesBread Bread (WheatBread a subclass). Instances: "big potato" (an Ingredient with property taste = sweet), a particular turkey sandwich. Then a query like "which veg sandwiches use wheat bread?" is a graph pattern, not a text search.

In a college ontology, "which faculty teach AI?" is answered by walking Faculty → teaches → Course nodes. Ontologies are agreed by communities so that data from many sources means the same thing.

sections.title: TBox, ABox and the knowledge graph
sections.plain: Separate the schema from the facts; combine them and you have a knowledge graph.
sections.body:
Description logics, the formal basis of OWL, distinguish:

  • TBox (terminological box): concepts and their relations: "every Student is a Person", "studiesAt links a Student to a College", "isInsideOf is transitive".
  • ABox (assertional box): facts about individuals: "Rahul is a Student", "Rahul studiesAt the college in Jaipur", "the Margherita costs 250".
ontology (TBox) + data (ABox) = knowledge graph

Keeping them separate lets the same schema serve millions of facts, and lets a reasoner check every new fact against the schema.

sections.title: OWL property types and reasoning
sections.plain: Declare logical properties of relations so a reasoner can infer new facts and catch contradictions.
sections.body:
The Web Ontology Language (OWL) adds expressive logic: individuals, class expressions, property assertions and characteristics:

constructmeaningexample
transitiveA→B and B→C ⇒ A→Cegg isInsideOf sandwich, sandwich isInsideOf lunchbox ⇒ egg isInsideOf lunchbox
symmetricA→B ⇒ B→Acheese pairsWith tomato ⇒ tomato pairsWith cheese
inversep(A, B) ⇔ q(B, A)sandwich contains cheese ⇔ cheese isIngredientOf sandwich
disjointnever both for the same pairhasWife and hasHusband

A reasoner applies these rules: it derives implicit facts and detects inconsistencies. If a graph contains both Ravi hasWife Meera and Ravi hasHusband Meera, each triple looks fine alone, but the disjointness axiom flags the contradiction, catching data-entry or extraction errors.

sections.title: The semantic-web layer stack
sections.plain: Identifiers, then facts, then shared vocabularies, then logic, then large connected data.
sections.body:
1. URIs: global identifiers (identity).
  2. RDF: triples and graphs (structure).
  3. RDFS and ontologies: classes, hierarchies, shared vocabularies (standardisation, hierarchy).
  4. OWL: logical characteristics and constraints (rules, reasoning).
  5. Knowledge graphs: ontology plus large instance data, queried by applications (data at scale).

Each layer fixes what the previous one couldn't: RDF gives structure but not agreed meaning; RDFS gives types but not logic; OWL gives logic; a KG puts it to work on real data. Query languages such as SPARQL (for RDF) and Cypher (for property-graph databases) sit on top.

sections.title: Building knowledge graphs at scale
sections.plain: Extract triples from text automatically, map them to an ontology, merge duplicates, and check them.
sections.body:
Hand-building is too slow for large graphs. Pipelines combine: named-entity recognition and linking (which real-world entity is "Apple"?), relation extraction (often over dependency paths, M10), and increasingly LLM-based triple extraction (prompt a model to output (subject, predicate, object) triples), plus ontology learning (proposing classes and properties from data).

Example: "Rahul studies AI at a college in Jaipur, Rajasthan" → (Rahul, type, Student), (Rahul, studies, AI), (AI, belongsTo, Computer Science), (Rahul, studiesAt, College), (College, locatedIn, Jaipur), (Jaipur, locatedIn, Rajasthan).

Quality steps: entity resolution (merge "HarperCollins" and "Harper Collins"), predicate normalisation to the ontology, provenance (which source said it), confidence scores, and reasoner checks, since LLM extraction can hallucinate relations. Large public examples: DBpedia (from Wikipedia infoboxes), Wikidata (community-edited) and the wider Linked Open Data cloud.

sections.title: Applications and graph databases
sections.plain: Knowledge graphs power search panels, recommendations, analytics and grounded AI answers.
sections.body:
Graph databases such as Neo4j store nodes and edges natively; Cypher queries express multi-hop patterns directly, e.g. MATCH (c)-[:ORDERED]->(p)-[:HAS_PRICE]->(x) WHERE x > 300 RETURN c, p.

Applications: knowledge panels in web search (facts about a person or place shown beside results), recommendation (users–items–attributes), fraud detection (rings of linked accounts), biomedical discovery, and enterprise data integration.

Community detection (e.g. the Louvain method, maximising modularity) finds densely connected clusters and can reveal hidden links between groups. Graph RAG retrieves facts and neighbourhoods from a KG to give an LLM verified context (M14). Knowledge graphs offer explicit, explainable, updatable facts; LLMs offer fluent language and broad coverage: their combination is the active frontier.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Open-world assumption: in RDF/OWL a missing fact is unknown, not false (unlike most databases).
  • RDF vs property graphs: RDF uses triples and URIs; property graphs (Neo4j) attach key–value properties to nodes and edges.
  • Reasoning cost: full OWL reasoning can be expensive; profiles (OWL EL, QL, RL) trade expressiveness for speed.
  • Embeddings for KGs: methods like TransE learn vectors where head + relation ≈ tail, enabling link prediction.

code.title: Triples, traversal and RDFS inference
code.explain: Stores the pizza facts as triples, answers 1-hop and 2-hop questions (Margherita; 250; who ordered veg), infers rdf:type Food/Product/Person through rdfs:subClassOf, and shows how mapping 'ordered'/'bought'/'placedOrderFor' to one vocabulary raises recall from 1/3 to 3/3.
mistakes: Inferring only one level of the class hierarchy.
Treating synonymous predicates as different relations.
code.notes: Pure Python; real systems use RDF stores and SPARQL.
code.output:
1-hop: what did Rahul order? ['Margherita']
2-hop: price of what Rahul ordered: ['250']
who ordered a veg pizza? ['Rahul']
inferred: ('Margherita', 'rdf:type', 'Food')
inferred: ('Margherita', 'rdf:type', 'Product')
inferred: ('Pepperoni', 'rdf:type', 'Food')
inferred: ('Pepperoni', 'rdf:type', 'Product')
inferred: ('Priya', 'rdf:type', 'Person')
inferred: ('Rahul', 'rdf:type', 'Person')
naive query for 'ordered' finds 1 of 3 orders
after mapping to one vocabulary: 3 of 3

code.title: OWL-style reasoning and community detection
code.explain: Computes the closure under transitive (egg isInsideOf lunchbox), symmetric and inverse properties, detects the hasWife/hasHusband disjointness violation, then builds a small graph and finds its 2-hop neighbourhood, a shortest path, and three Louvain communities.
mistakes: Stopping the closure before a fixed point.
Expecting community labels to be stable across seeds.
code.notes: A minimal rule engine, not a full OWL reasoner.

inferred: ('cheese', 'isIngredientOf', 'sandwich')
inferred: ('egg', 'isInsideOf', 'lunchbox')
inferred: ('tomato', 'pairsWith', 'cheese')
